1093.title: Many rites (CCC 1200–1206)
1093.hook: Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite, Chaldean: one faith, many forms
1093.howItsDone: Roman-rite parishes celebrate the Mass, while Byzantine Catholic parishes celebrate what they call the Divine Liturgy; each Eastern Catholic church keeps its own liturgy, calendar and customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the church building, and the ambo, where the word of God is proclaimed. Your line was each place speaks.

Two Catholic churches, one Sunday morning, a few streets apart. In the first, the priest stands at a plain altar facing the people, and an organ plays. In the second, painted icons stretch across the front, incense hangs in the air, and nearly everything is sung, back and forth between priest and people. The prayers are different. The vestments are different. Even the name is different: in the second church people may call it the Divine Liturgy. Yet both are Catholic, both are in communion with the Pope, and both celebrate the same Eucharist. How?
screen: `TWO CHURCHES, ONE SUNDAY.` → `ORGAN HERE, ICONS AND INCENSE THERE.` → `BOTH CATHOLIC.`

segments.voice: Day nine hundred forty-three met one Eastern Catholic church; today, the bigger picture. The word is rite. In ordinary speech a rite is a ceremony. In the Catechism it means something bigger: a whole family of worship, with its own prayers, music, calendar and ways, handed down in one part of the Church. The Catechism starts with what doesn't change: the one mystery of Christ, his death and resurrection, celebrated everywhere. Then a striking claim: that mystery is so rich that no single liturgical tradition can say all of it. As the Gospel traveled, it took root among different peoples, and their worship grew in harmony with their languages and cultures. The Catechism names the traditions in use today. The Latin, mainly the Roman rite, along with some local and religious-order rites. The Byzantine. The Alexandrian, or Coptic. The Syriac. The Armenian. The Maronite. The Chaldean. Repeating the Second Vatican Council, it says the Church holds all lawfully recognized rites to be of equal right and dignity, and wants to keep them alive and growing. Not a main rite and some exotic extras. Equal. But there's a limit: diversity mustn't damage unity. The rites stay one by keeping the same apostolic faith, the same sacraments, and communion with the bishops and the Pope. So the icons and the organ aren't rivals. They're two ways of saying one thing, each fully at home in the one Church.
screen: `A RITE: A WHOLE FAMILY OF WORSHIP.` · `ONE MYSTERY, TOO RICH FOR ONE FORM.` · `EQUAL RIGHT AND DIGNITY.` · `DIVERSITY MUST NOT HARM UNITY.`

Rite. Not one ceremony but a whole tradition of worship, with its own prayers and ways, celebrating the one mystery of Christ. Today's word.
Your line: one faith, many forms. Equal right, equal dignity. Rest well.

1094.title: Baptism's rite (CCC 1234–1245)
1094.hook: sign of the cross, word, exorcism, water, chrism, white garment, candle
1094.howItsDone: In the Latin rite a priest or deacon usually baptizes, in a parish church, with parents and godparents present; the family receives the white garment and a candle lit from the Easter candle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many rites: Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian and the rest, each a whole family of worship. Your line was one faith, many forms.

In some homes there's a drawer with a small white cloth folded inside, and next to it a fat candle that's been lit exactly once. Nobody uses them. Nobody throws them away either. They're souvenirs of a few minutes at a font, often from before their owner could remember anything. A Catholic baptism isn't just water. It's a short drama in several acts.
screen: `A WHITE CLOTH IN A DRAWER.` → `A CANDLE LIT ONCE.` → `A DRAMA IN SEVERAL ACTS.`

segments.voice: Day one hundred twenty-six met the water; today, the whole rite. The Catechism says baptism's meaning shows up in its rite, so follow it. It begins with the sign of the cross traced on the person about to belong to Christ, marking them with the cross that saved them. Then the word of God is read, because baptism is the sacrament of faith, and faith comes from hearing. Then a prayer of exorcism, asking that the person be freed from sin and the power of evil, with an anointing; and the person, or for a child the parents and godparents, renounce Satan and profess the faith of the Church. Then the water is blessed, asking the Holy Spirit to come into it. The water goes on three times, by immersion or by pouring over the head, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Those words come from the end of Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus sends the apostles out, in the Douay-Rheims: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." After the water, three signs explain what happened. An anointing with sacred chrism, the perfumed oil a bishop blesses, for a person now anointed by the Holy Spirit. A white garment, because, as Paul writes, "as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ." And a candle lit from the Easter candle: Christ has given this person light, to be light for the world. Then, at the altar, the newly baptized are led in the Our Father, and a blessing ends the rite.
screen: `MARKED WITH THE CROSS.` · `WORD, RENUNCIATION, FAITH.` · `WATER, THREE TIMES.` · `CHRISM, GARMENT, CANDLE.` · then, large: `HAVE PUT ON CHRIST.`

Your line: the white garment. The water, then the signs that explain it. See you tomorrow.

1095.title: Baptism and hope (CCC 1257–1261)
1095.hook: God is bound to the sacraments, but he himself is not bound by them
1095.howItsDone: The Church celebrates funeral rites for children whose parents wanted them baptized but who died before baptism, commending them to God's mercy; Catholics may pray for anyone who has died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baptism's rite: the cross, the water three times, the chrism, the candle. Your line was the white garment.

"Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." That's Jesus speaking to Nicodemus at night, in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims. For the Catholic Church, baptism is necessary. Then the question. What about everyone who was never baptized? The grandmother of another faith. The friend who never heard the Gospel in a way that made sense. The baby who died before anyone could reach the font. The Catechism doesn't dodge it.
screen: `BORN AGAIN OF WATER AND THE SPIRIT.` → `WHAT ABOUT EVERYONE ELSE?` → `THE CATECHISM ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: It starts firmly. Baptism is necessary for salvation for those to whom the Gospel has been proclaimed and who could ask for it. The Church knows of no other means than baptism to make sure of entry into eternal happiness, so she won't neglect the mission to baptize. God has bound salvation to the sacrament of baptism, the Catechism says, but he himself is not bound by his sacraments. The Church is bound to them. God is free. Then, widening circles. First, those who die for the faith without being baptized: tradition calls this a baptism of blood, and their death joins them to Christ. Second, catechumens, people preparing for baptism who die before the day comes. Their desire for it, with repentance and love, gives them what the sacrament would have given. Third, and wider: every person who doesn't know the Gospel of Christ and his Church, but seeks the truth and does the will of God as they understand it, can be saved. The Catechism supposes such people would have wanted baptism had they known it was needed. And last, the hardest: children who die without baptism. Here the Church can only entrust them to the mercy of God, as she does in her funeral rites for them. Then it points to God's mercy, which desires all to be saved, and to Jesus's tenderness toward children. In the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not." Those, it says, allow us to hope. Not certainty. Hope.
screen: `BAPTISM IS NECESSARY.` · `GOD IS NOT BOUND BY HIS SACRAMENTS.` · `BLOOD, DESIRE, THE SEEKER.` · `CHILDREN ENTRUSTED TO MERCY.` · then, large: `SUFFER THE LITTLE CHILDREN TO COME UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who was never baptized: a friend, a grandparent, a colleague, or a child who died too soon. If you pray, place them in silence into God's mercy, the way the Church does for its little ones; if you don't, hold them with care, and let that be enough. If that loss is heavy right now, please reach out: call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help.

Your line: God is not bound. The last word belongs to him. I'll be here tomorrow.

1096.title: Confirmation's gifts (CCC 1302–1305)
1096.hook: it deepens baptismal grace, strengthens, and sends
1096.howItsDone: In the Latin rite the bishop usually confirms, anointing the forehead with chrism; candidates choose a sponsor and often a saint's name. In the Eastern Catholic churches the sacrament, called chrismation, is given right after baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism and hope: baptism is necessary, yet the Church entrusts to mercy those who never received it. Your line was God is not bound.

A line forms in the center aisle. Teenagers in their best clothes, a few adults, each with a sponsor standing close behind, a hand on the shoulder. At the front, the bishop. One by one they step up. He calls each by the name they've chosen, dips his thumb in oil, traces a cross on the forehead, says a few words about the gift of the Holy Spirit, and wishes them peace. Afterward there are photos and cake. But the Catechism says something was given in that moment, and that it pushes outward.
screen: `A LINE IN THE CENTER AISLE.` → `OIL, A CROSS, A FEW WORDS.` → `WHAT WAS GIVEN?`

segments.voice: Day one hundred twenty-seven met the oil and the seal; today, what they do. The Catechism calls the effect of Confirmation a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit, like the one the apostles received at Pentecost, and it moves in three ways. First, it deepens. Confirmation doesn't replace baptism; it brings baptismal grace to growth. It roots a person more deeply as a child of God, who can call God Father. It unites them more firmly to Christ, and binds them more closely to the Church. It increases the gifts of the Holy Spirit, gifts named from Isaiah's picture of the promised king, in the Douay-Rheims: "the spirit of counsel, and of fortitude." Second, it strengthens: a special strength of the Spirit to spread and defend the faith in word and action, to confess Christ's name boldly, and never to be ashamed of the cross. Third, it sends. Just before the Ascension, in Acts, Jesus tells the apostles they'll receive the power of the Holy Spirit, "and you shall be witnesses unto me." That's the direction of the whole sacrament: out the door. Like baptism, Confirmation is given only once. It leaves an indelible spiritual mark, a seal, a sign that Christ has claimed this person with his Spirit. Quoting Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says the confirmed receive the power to profess their faith publicly, almost as an official duty. So the oil on the forehead isn't an ending. It's a sending, and the cake is the send-off.
screen: `A SPECIAL OUTPOURING OF THE SPIRIT.` · `IT DEEPENS BAPTISM.` · `IT STRENGTHENS FOR WITNESS.` · `IT SENDS, AND IT SEALS ONCE.` · then, large: `YOU SHALL BE WITNESSES UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you go quiet about something you care about: a table where you change the subject, a group chat where you don't type what you think, a friend you haven't been honest with. If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit for courage there, in the Church's old words, Come, Holy Spirit, or in silence; if you don't, notice what courage would look like in that one place.
Confirmation's gifts. It deepens the grace of baptism, strengthens a person to witness, and sends them, sealed once and for good. Today's word.
Your line: sent. The cross on the forehead points out the door. Go gently.

1097.title: Names of the Eucharist (CCC 1328–1332)
1097.hook: Lord's Supper, breaking of bread, holy sacrifice, Holy Communion, Holy Mass
1097.howItsDone: Catholics in the Latin rite usually say Mass for the celebration and Holy Communion for receiving; Eastern Catholics speak of the Divine Liturgy, and the reserved Eucharist is called the Blessed Sacrament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Confirmation's gifts: it deepens, strengthens and sends. Your line was sent.

Evening, on the road to a village called Emmaus. Two disciples are walking out of Jerusalem, heartbroken, and a stranger falls in beside them. He explains the Scriptures to them all the way there. They beg him to stay for supper. At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them, and in that moment they recognize him, and he vanishes. That same hour they go back to Jerusalem to tell the others. Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, puts it this way: "they knew him in the breaking of bread." That phrase became one of the names for what Catholics celebrate at every Mass. Only one of them.
screen: `TWO DISCIPLES, A STRANGER.` → `BREAD BLESSED AND BROKEN.` → `THEY KNEW HIM.`

segments.voice: This path walked that road on day sixty-nine; today, the names. The Catechism says this sacrament is so rich that no one name can hold it, and each name brings something out. Eucharist means thanksgiving, tied to the Greek words in the Last Supper accounts, where Jesus gives thanks, and to the Jewish blessings that praise God over bread and wine. The Lord's Supper, because of the meal Jesus ate with his disciples the night before he died, and because it looks ahead to the wedding feast of the Lamb. The breaking of bread, the Emmaus name. In Acts it's what the first Christians kept doing; the Douay-Rheims says they persevered "in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." The memorial of the Lord's Passion and Resurrection. The Holy Sacrifice, because it makes present the one sacrifice of Christ. The Holy and Divine Liturgy, because the Church's whole liturgy finds its center here. The Most Blessed Sacrament, the name for the Eucharist kept in the tabernacle. Holy Communion, because through it people are united to Christ, and to each other in one body. And last, Holy Mass. The name comes from the end of the liturgy, the Catechism says, from the Latin word for sending, missio, because the people are sent out to do God's will in their daily lives. So the familiar name comes from the last line, the dismissal. Each name opens a different window on one thing: thanks, a supper, bread broken, a memorial, a sacrifice, communion, a sending.
screen: `EUCHARIST: THANKSGIVING.` · `THE SUPPER, THE BREAKING OF BREAD.` · `SACRIFICE, LITURGY, COMMUNION.` · `MASS: FROM THE SENDING.`

1098.title: Sacrifice and memorial (CCC 1362–1372)
1098.hook: the one sacrifice of Christ made present, not repeated
1098.howItsDone: At each Mass the priest repeats Christ's words over the bread and wine; the congregation is invited to offer their own lives with Christ's offering, and Masses are often offered for the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the names of the Eucharist: thanksgiving, the breaking of bread, Holy Communion, Mass. Your line was one gift, many names.

Is the Mass a fresh sacrifice every time? It's a fair question, asked sincerely or as a challenge. At Mass, a priest takes bread and wine and says the words Jesus said at the Last Supper. If that's a sacrifice, is Christ being offered again and again? The Catechism's answer hangs on one small Greek word in Jesus's command at the Last Supper, and it doesn't mean quite what English means by remember.
screen: `A FRESH SACRIFICE EVERY TIME?` → `THE WORDS OF THE LAST SUPPER.` → `ONE SMALL GREEK WORD.`

segments.voice: At the Last Supper, in Luke's Gospel, Jesus takes the bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Commemoration, or memorial. Behind it is the Greek anamnesis. In Scripture, the Catechism says, a memorial isn't only recalling the past. It proclaims what God has done, and in the liturgy those events become, in a certain way, present and real. Think of Passover: each time Israel celebrates it, the Exodus is made present to the memory of believers, so they shape their lives by it. So when the Church keeps the memorial of Christ's Passover, his death and resurrection, that event is made present. The one sacrifice Christ offered once for all on the cross stays present. That's why the Eucharist is also a sacrifice. Not because something new happens to Christ, but because it makes present the sacrifice of the cross, is its memorial, and applies its fruit. The Catechism is careful here. Christ's sacrifice and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice. The victim is one and the same: the Christ who offered himself on the cross now offers, through the ministry of priests. Only the manner differs: on the cross with blood, at the altar without. And the Church joins in: the Pope, the bishops and the whole people unite their praise, sufferings and work to his offering, and the saints in heaven join in it too. It's offered for the dead as well. So the answer to the hook is no. Not repeated. Present.

segments.voice: Picture the moment in the Mass when the priest repeats the words of the Last Supper and lifts up the host. 1099.title: The real presence (CCC 1373–1381)
1099.hook: Christ present in the word, the priest, the people, and above all under the species
1099.howItsDone: In Latin-rite churches people customarily genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering or leaving a pew, and some parishes hold Eucharistic adoration, with the host displayed in a monstrance for silent prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacrifice and memorial, and the word anamnesis. Your line was present, not repeated.

A man in a work jacket comes in out of the rain, dips his fingers in the holy water, walks halfway down the aisle, and stops. His right knee goes down to the floor for a second, his eyes on a small gold box at the front with a lamp burning beside it. He didn't kneel to the altar, or the crowd, or the building. He knelt toward that box, because of what the Church teaches is kept inside it. Today's word is the reason for that knee.
screen: `IN FROM THE RAIN.` → `ONE KNEE TO THE FLOOR.` → `TOWARD A SMALL GOLD BOX.`

segments.voice: Day ninety-nine taught the knee itself; now, the why. Christ is present to his Church in many ways, the Catechism says. In his word. In the Church's prayer, because he said, in the Douay-Rheims, "where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." In the poor, the sick, the imprisoned. In the sacraments. In the sacrifice of the Mass, and in the person of the priest. But above all, he is present under the Eucharistic species, the bread and wine, and that presence the Catechism calls unique. Quoting the Council of Trent, it says the body and blood of Christ, with his soul and divinity, the whole Christ, are contained in the sacrament truly, really, and substantially. Three words, each shutting a door. Truly: not as a picture. Really: not only in the mind of the believer. Substantially: in what the bread and wine are, not just how they look. The Church calls this change transubstantiation. The presence begins at the consecration and lasts as long as the species do, and Christ is whole and entire in each of them and in every part. Behind it all is Jesus's line in John's Gospel: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." So the Church shows adoration by genuflecting or bowing deeply, and keeps the Eucharist in the tabernacle, for the sick and for prayer. Quoting Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says this presence can't be grasped by the senses, only by faith. That's the knee in the aisle.
screen: `MANY WAYS PRESENT.` · `ABOVE ALL, UNDER BREAD AND WINE.` · `TRULY, REALLY, SUBSTANTIALLY.` · `KNEELING, AND KEPT FOR PRAYER.` · then, large: `MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED.`

segments.voice: If you're near a church, find the tabernacle with its lamp and bend one knee slowly, as if for the first time; if not, do it where you are, or simply bow your head, the deep bow the Catechism names too. Then sit and say the three words, one per breath: truly, really, substantially. If you pray, stay in adoration a while; if you don't, just notice what it's like to kneel to something.
Real presence. Christ present in many ways, and above all under the bread and wine: truly, really, substantially. Today's word.
Your line: truly, really, substantially. Seven days, from many rites to the real presence. See you tomorrow.
